title: Axial resin duct quantification in tree rings: A functional defense trait
author: Hood, Reed, et al.

steps.title: Collect cores with appropriate borer
steps.instruction: Use a 5.15 mm increment borer to collect two cores per tree, or a 10 mm or 12 mm borer to collect one core per tree; larger 10–12 mm borers are also useful for dead or rotted trees.

steps.title: Store cores for drying
steps.instruction: Place 5.15 mm cores in sturdy paper straws (e.g., Aardvark Straws, Ft. Wayne, IN, USA) and bundle the straws with newspaper; for 10–12 mm cores, insert them into 12.6 mm (0.5 in) PVC pipe, seal ends with masking tape, label, and drill small holes to allow airflow.

steps.title: Dry cores
steps.instruction: Air‑dry cores for about one week (time varies with humidity and temperature) in the permeable storage; if time is limited, oven‑dry in the same straws or PVC pipes at 50–60 °C for 1–2 days until no shrinkage occurs after mounting.

steps.title: Mount dried cores correctly
steps.instruction: Orient each core so the transverse (cross‑section) face is upward; the jagged lines from ripped tracheids must be on the sides of the mounted core. If the lines are not visible, roll the core back and forth between hands, look for glimmering light on the sides, and verify that tracheids are vertical at the end.

steps.title: Sand core surfaces
steps.instruction: Using a belt sander, sand each core sequentially with 120, 220, 320, then 400 grit sandpaper, never skipping a grit. After each grit, remove all scratches before proceeding to the next.

substeps.instruction: Let the core and sander cool between grit changes to avoid resin smearing.
Do not sand for prolonged periods to prevent heat buildup.

steps.title: Polish and clean surfaces
steps.instruction: Hand‑polish the sanded surface with 40, 30, 15, and finally 9 µm polishing paper, removing scratches from the previous grit each time; frequently inspect the surface with a hand lens or dissecting scope. After polishing, blow off dust with compressed air.

steps.title: Cross‑date rings and annotate
steps.instruction: Assign calendar years to each ring, marking decadal years, missing or false rings with pencil marks on the core before scanning; consult standard cross‑dating references for detailed procedures.

steps.title: Measure axial resin ducts
steps.instruction: Capture images of the prepared surface and record the number of axial resin ducts (including lumen and surrounding epithelial cells) for each ring, entering the data into a TXT file immediately after imaging.

steps.title: Perform quality control
steps.instruction: At each major step (drying, mounting, sanding, measurement) verify accuracy; after measuring a core, add the corresponding years to the resin‑duct file right away, correcting any year‑alignment errors by editing the TXT file or re‑measuring the core. Once the master chronology is assembled, plot the data to spot implausibly large or small values.

steps.title: Archive data publicly
steps.instruction: Upload the final resin‑duct chronology and associated metadata to a public repository such as the International Tree‑Ring Databank (ITRDB).

description: We find it easiest to conduct quality assessments at each major step rather than waiting until the end. An accurate ring width file is the foundation for building the final resin duct chronology and time should be spent to ensure that all cores included are datable for the time period of interest. As noted above, we recommend adding years to each resin duct file immediately after duct measurement is completed for an individual core rather than in batches, and have thus set up Section 1 of the R script to function in this way. This will reduce time spent correcting errors in years not aligning correctly because the image of the core in question is still fresh in your mind. If an error in years occurs, you can either correct it by hand in the TXT file or redo the resin duct measurements for that core. We find it easier to correct the TXT file by inserting year breaks, deleting double counted ducts, etc. rather than starting over in ImageJ. After the master resin duct chronology is created, basic data plotting will allow checking for implausibly large or small values. We encourage archiving data in a publicly accessible repository such as the International Tree-Ring Databank (ITRDB; https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/data-access/paleoclimatology-data/datasets/tree-ring). The ITRDB now allows inclusion of resin duct chronologies.
